activities.caption: true or false — the naming and the language
activities.name: webNameJudge

statements.s: JavaScript is a browser version of Java.
statements.why: The shared name was a 1995 marketing alliance: Java is class-based and compiled to bytecode; JavaScript is dynamically typed and prototype-based.

statements.s: JavaScript was built at Netscape in a famous ten-day sprint to make pages react.
statements.why: History's fastest language birth — and the naming has been confusing people ever since.

statements.s: Java fluency transfers directly to JavaScript.
statements.why: They share C-style syntax the way many modern languages do — and little else.

statements.s: Functions in JavaScript are values — assignable, passable, returnable.
statements.why: Which is why callbacks, event handlers and framework components are all functions in transit.

activities.anchor: Pair it with the browser's second core rule
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the three pillars of browser security
activities.name: webPillarsCloze

config.text: The web's three-pillar security model: %%0%% isolation (one site's script cannot read another's data), %%1%% transport (HTTPS, the TLS of the networking lesson), and %%2%% boundaries (escape user text before it enters the page).
config.hint: Name all three — each pillar answers a different kind of attack.

activities.anchor: larger per-origin key–value stores usable by scripts
activities.caption: find the faulty line — where state lives
activities.name: webStorageSpot

config.prompt: A summary of the state homes contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: HTTP is stateless, so continuity must be reassembled every time.
Cookies are server-issued pairs the browser replays on every request to that site.
HttpOnly keeps cookies away from JavaScript — a direct XSS mitigation.
localStorage is the right home for session tokens, being larger and per-origin.
SameSite curbs cross-site request forgery by not sending cookies on third-party requests.
config.correction: Web storage is convenient for preferences and WRONG for session tokens — readable by any injected script; identity belongs in HttpOnly cookies, UI state in the client, durable truth in the database.
config.why: State has designated homes — small rules, strictly enforced, doing enormous work.

activities.caption: place each piece of state in its home
activities.name: webStateBranch

config.root: You are adding 'remember my dark-mode preference' and 'stay logged in' to an app. Walk where each piece of state lives.

start.text: The login session token. Where does it go?

choices.label: An HttpOnly cookie
choices.feedback: Right: the browser replays it, JavaScript can never read it, and the Secure flag restricts it to HTTPS.

choices.label: localStorage, for easy access from scripts
choices.feedback: Convenient and wrong: any injected script reads it — one XSS and the session is stolen.

local.text: The stolen session shows why homes matter. Now the dark-mode preference?

choices.label: localStorage — client-side UI state
choices.feedback: Right: preferences are UI state in the client — scripts reading them is fine.

choices.label: A database table
choices.feedback: Possible, but heavier than needed — UI state in the client, durable truth in the database.

cookie.text: Identity secured. And the dark-mode preference?

choices.label: localStorage — client-side UI state
choices.feedback: Right: preferences are client-side UI state.

choices.label: An HttpOnly cookie too
choices.feedback: Cookies replay on every request to that site — a preference would ride along forever; the client is the right home.

ui.text: The rule of thumb: identity in HttpOnly cookies, UI state in the client, durable truth in the database — anything else is state you have misplaced.

db.text: Durable truth does belong in the database — but a theme preference is UI state; carry it in the client.

overkill.text: A preference in a cookie rides every request forever — the client is the right home.

config.why: Small rules, strictly enforced, doing enormous work — misplace the state and you will find it in a bug report.

activities.caption: which curve is the compositor-owned animation?
activities.name: webFrameTrace

config.prompt: Frame cost against time during two animations — which curve belongs to the one running on the compositor?
config.why: Those animated effects ride hardware planes — flat cost; top/left changes re-run geometry every frame and the cost sawtooths.
